shows.title: Subtracting and Subtracting Again
shows.description:
Kim Hodeuk has spent decades pushing traditional Korean ink painting toward something closer to pure gesture, and this show finds him paring the medium down even further. Rather than filling the canvas, he works by subtraction — bold, splattered strokes set against raw, unprimed canvas so that the yeobaek, the traditional "empty" ground of ink painting, becomes an active field of energy rather than passive background.

The exhibition extends the artist's ink practice into immersive spatial installation, letting his brushwork spill off the paper and into the room itself. It's a fitting move for an artist whose whole vocabulary is built on momentum and release: bold splashes of ink meant to evoke natural forces — waterfalls, wind, the physical charge of a body moving fast across a surface — rather than depict them literally.

Kim, born in Daegu in 1950, is one of the senior figures of contemporary Korean ink painting, known for a style that treats brush and paper almost like a percussion instrument — fast, forceful, intuitive. He has shown extensively in Korea including at Hakgojae Gallery and previously at Artside itself, and his recent work has taken on a rawer, more urgent quality that observers connect to his own health struggles in recent years. This show is a chance to see a senior painter still finding new extremity in a technique he has practiced for half a century.

shows.title: 1 day in space
shows.description:
Ed Atkins built his reputation on uncanny CGI avatars that stood in for a very analog kind of grief, so it's notable that the inaugural show at Gladstone's new Hannam-dong space finds him putting the digital surrogate aside. 1 day in space centers on a new video, 16th of April 2026, 19.21′30″ (Passive Mech), a thirty-minute timelapse Atkins shot through his daughter's bedroom window as a cardboard stage set slowly collapses outside — a blunt, almost domestic meditation on time passing and images arriving too late to hold onto anything.

Around the video, Atkins fills the galleries with frottage drawings, photographic c-type prints dated and time-stamped like diary entries, and small cardboard sculptures and dioramas built from the debris of the same backyard set. Family photographs, some inherited (one piece incorporates a childhood work by the artist's own father), get folded into the same visual language of glue, cardboard, and graphite rubbing, so that inherited memory and manufactured stage-set start to look like the same material.

It's a quieter, more handmade Atkins than the one known for hyperreal digital doubles, but the underlying preoccupations — the gap between an image and the moment it claims to preserve, the strange tenderness of watching something decay — are the same. As the opening exhibition of Gladstone's expanded two-floor Seoul outpost, designed by Minsuk Cho, it's also a statement about what the gallery wants its new home to do: give room-scale, research-heavy solo shows the space to breathe.

shows.title: Theaster Gates: Seoul (2026)
shows.description:
White Cube Seoul's next show brings Theaster Gates to Korea for the first time, following the gallery's current Marina Rheingantz exhibition. Gates is a Chicago-based artist, archivist and urban planner whose work moves between sculpture, ceramics, painting and large-scale social practice — he's as well known for revitalizing derelict buildings on Chicago's South Side as for the tar-and-roofing-material paintings and glazed stoneware vessels he shows in galleries.

Details of the Seoul presentation are still under wraps, but Gates's practice consistently returns to questions of Black cultural memory, labor and material reclamation: repurposed wood, fire hose, tar paper and clay worked with the same hands-on attention he brings to community buildings. Expect an exhibition of new work that continues his long-running interest in how objects carry history and how art spaces can double as sites of gathering.

This is a show to watch for rather than one to describe in detail yet — it's included here because White Cube's own site confirms it is coming to the Seoul space this fall, but exact dates were not yet published at the time of writing.
